blocks.text: The same point is supported by the fact that the Arabs record two species of venomous stellio, which differ only in size. The larger is called سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] sammabras, and the smaller [col. 1087] وزغة [wazagha] vvezga. In the name sammabras, compounded of سام [sām] and ابرص [abraṣ], the first part is shortened from semamith and means venomous; the second means leprous, or marked with spots of leprosy. So, literally, sammabras is leprous semamith, or a species of lizard notable for venom and for spots of leprosy. For two things are to be noted in the stellio: first, that it is venomous, which has already been treated; second, that it is leprous, that is, marked with spots as if of leprosy. The Arabic SAMMABRAS contains both of these, the Hebrew SEMAMITH only the first. Damir: وانما سمي هذا النوع سام ابرص لانه سم اي جعل الله فيه السم وجعله ابرص [wa-innamā summiya hādhā al-nawʿ sām abraṣ li-annahu summa ay jaʿala Allāh fīhi al-summ wa-jaʿalahu abraṣ] This species of lizard indeed has the name sammabras, [II, 515] because it is venomous, that is, God put venom in it, and (moreover) made it leprous ^{(1)}. The Romans called the stellio's spots by a more honourable name, stellae [stars], whence the animal itself is called stellio. Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 5, fable 7:
— — — — and it has a name suited to its colour, its body starred with varied drops.

Salonius on Proverbs: What kind of animal is the stellio? A kind of lizard, very sluggish and of varied colour. ' Hence it got the name stellio, because it is marked and variegated as if with stellae, that is, drops. Here he follows the Poet in such a way that he seems to have taken stellae [stars] for stillae [drops], or guttae [drops]. By the opposite error many explain מרים Marjam, the Syrian name of Mary, as maris stella [star of the sea] instead of maris stilla [drop of the sea]. Pliny also calls them lentigines [freckles], when he writes of the Greek stellio in book 29, chapter 4: This one is full of freckles. Hence a freckled eunuch is called by Menander γαλεώτης [galeōtēs], that is, stellio, because of the spots on his face. Terence in the Eunuch ^{d)} wrongly rendered this colore mustelino [of weasel colour], as if γαλεώτης [galeōtēs] were named ἀπὸ τῆς γαλῆς [apo tēs galēs], that is, from the weasel, as Donatus observes there.

[II, 516] In Alkazuini, sammabras is defined as الوزغ الصغير الراس الطويل الذنب [al-wazagh al-ṣaghīr al-raʾs al-ṭawīl al-dhanab] alvvezgo (or stellio) with a small head and a long tail. In Damir and Alcamus, an animal من كبار الوزغ [min kibār al-wazagh] of the large guezgi, or stellios. The Arabs tell the fable that leprosy was inflicted on it as punishment for a crime it committed, namely because with its breath it kindled the fire into which Abraham was thrown. They add that leprosy is produced by eating salt in which it has rolled, or on which it has discharged slime. Hence this animal is most hateful to the Arabs ^{(2)}. And Iahius, son of Iamer, says that he holds dearer one who has killed a hundred stellios than one who has redeemed ماية رقبة [māya raqaba] a hundred necks, that is, a hundred slaves. Many sayings of Muhammad are cited on this matter. Nor was the stellio less hateful to the ancient Greeks. Antoninus Liberalis, in the passage cited above on the stellio: Ὑπὸ Θεῶν καὶ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων μεμίσηται· ὁ δ' ἀποκτείνας κεχαρισμένος γίνεται Δημῆτρι [Hypo Theōn kai hypo anthrōpōn memisētai; ho d' apokteinas kecharismenos ginetai Dēmētri]. It is hateful to gods and men; and he who kills it does a thing pleasing to Ceres. Yet it is useful for many things, which do not belong here. But I cannot fail to note what Alkazuini has in the chapter On sammabras: لحمه يوضع علي لسع العقرب ينفع نفعا بينا [laḥmuhu yūḍaʿ ʿalī lasʿ al-ʿaqrab yanfaʿ nafʿan bayyinan] Its flesh, when placed on a scorpion's [col. 1088] sting, is of evident benefit. So also Damir. It is thus established that it is the same animal as the stellio discussed above, although Avicenna sometimes uses the word for the common lizard.

Now, if what Solomon says of the semamith is examined, everything will be found to fit the stellio. There are four things, he says, little upon the earth (the Greeks ἐλάχιστα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [elachista epi tēs gēs]), yet wise, as if taught wisdom. Among these the stellio is rightly counted, a small animal and very clever ^{(3)}. On its small stature Ovid writes thus:
And it is contracted into a small form, lest it have great power to harm, and its size is less than a small lizard.
Claudian, or whoever is the author of the Sorrows of Ceres:
Spots appear, its form is small, a tail smeared on rises, and it imitates the wandering limbs of a tiny lizard.
Porphyry in Eusebius, book 5 of the Praeparatio, [II, 517] Ζώοισιν λεπτοίσι κατοικιδίοις σκαλαβώταις [Zōoisin leptoisi katoikidiois skalabōtais], To small little animals, domestic stellios.
